IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01518

But to meditate on them as signs (âyât) taking place “within the soul” is to experience and verify something else: the true Self coming to birth in the divine center of your being is the spiritual child of your “heart.” In other words, the “Muhammad of your being” is the spiritual offspring of the “Abraham of your being.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01519

Thus, within the person as microcosm, one realizes the truth of the claim that Muhammad's religion has its origin in Abraham's religion. For “Abraham was neither Jew nor Christian; he was a pure believer (hanîf), a moslim” (3:60). That is to say, the “Abraham of your being” is led through the subtle centers of higher consciousness and the hidden mystery—the Moses and Jesus of your being—avoiding the errors that threaten their people, meaning the faculties of each center, until he reaches the center that embodies his spiritual offspring: your true Self.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01520

This is how every teaching and event of the Qur'an must be meditated upon, brought inward, and given its ta'wîl: its “return,” its exegesis, its turning from the “world of horizons” to the “world of the soul.” Every word addressed to one of the seven prophets, every word spoken by them, every event in which they act, must be understood as taking place within the “subtle centers” that each prophet embodies. This prophetic pattern of the centers or organs of the subtle human constitution opens up extraordinary possibilities for inward realization.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01521

Semnani writes: “Whenever you hear in the Book the words addressed to Adam, hear them through the corresponding organ of your subtle body (latîfa qâlabîya) ... Meditate on what it symbolizes, and be certain that the inner meaning of the discourse concerns you, as a discourse about the world of the soul, just as its outer meaning concerns Adam in the world of horizons ... Only then will you be able to apply the teaching of the divine Word to yourself, and gather it like a branch still laden with flowers.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01522

“Whenever you hear or meditate on the verses concerning Noah, hear them through the subtle organ of your vital soul (latîfa nafsîya), so that you, too, will not be overwhelmed by the waters of the flood or held captive in the double hell of lust and violence, and so that the people of your faculties will not be swallowed up in the depths of illusory desires. Whenever you hear the verses revealed about Abraham, hear them through the subtle organ of your heart (latîfa qalbîya).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01523

“Attend to the words addressed to you by the divine Friend; take care not to become absorbed in anything else, so that, leading you from signs perceived by the senses to signs grasped by the understanding, he may become your only Guide as well. Whenever you hear the words addressed to Moses during his ‘secret conversations’ (monâjât), or anything concerning Moses' spiritual states, receive them through the subtle organ of your higher consciousness (latîfa sirrîya), the Moses of your being.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01524

“Take care to fulfill what those words implicitly require, lest the Samaritan lead the people of your faculties astray with the golden calf of unruly passions. And whenever you meditate on the verses that name David, on the divine visitations flowing from the Attribute of Love, perceive all of this through the subtle organ of your Spirit (latîfa rûhîya), the David of your being. He was taught the art of making coats of mail, which signify the gentle inspirations of love beneath the rigid appearance of servitude.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01525

“Then the people of your faculties will be protected from the sword of lies, the lance of conjecture, and the arrow of doubt; and you will make your body act through the action of the Spirit that uses it.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01526

“Whenever you meditate on what concerns the spiritual states of Jesus, hear it through the subtle organ of your ‘hidden mystery’ (latîfa khafîya), that is, through the Jesus of your being.” What we must understand here is profoundly serious. In a Qur'anic question addressed to Jesus, Semnani finds, at the level of the subtle organ embodied by Jesus, the reason why certain mystics in Islam and Christians in general have fallen into an illusion springing from the same source.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01527

“Was it you,” Jesus is asked, “who ever said to the people: Take me and my mother as two gods apart from God?—By Your glory, no! [Jesus answers.] How could I say something unworthy of me?” (5:116). Neither Jesus son of Mary nor the “Jesus of your being,” then, is responsible for the failing of his people—a failing that Semnani understands with extraordinary insight, and for which he proposes an equally extraordinary spiritual remedy.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01528

A study remains to be written of this criticism of Christianity as it appeared to one of Sufism's most profound masters. Needless to say, it differs entirely from the polemics of official apologists and scholars concerned only with outward doctrine. Its tone is impassioned, in keeping with the spiritual stakes as Semnani sees them. To understand it, we must turn to his commentary on Sura 112, one of the final suras of the Qur'an.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01529

There he senses a striking connection between the temptation to which, in his view, Christian dogma succumbed when it proclaimed Christ, son of Mary, to be God, and the mystical intoxication in which Hallaj cried “I am God,” while Bastami declared “Glory be to me! How exalted is my state!” When the mystic emerges from this intoxication, horrified by a boldness for which the overwhelming experience of the divine affords some excuse, he seeks refuge in the desire to annihilate himself and thereby atone for the blasphemy: “Kill me, my companions!
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01530

“For to live is death to me, and to die is life”. The mystic then faces an acutely dangerous situation. He needs the help of a shaykh of great experience to draw him out of the abyss into which his consciousness threatens to collapse, and to lead him to a higher station—the station that truly is the divine center of his being (latîfa haqqîya).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01531

In Semnani's view, the Christian needs spiritual healing of the same kind. For beneath both manifestations of the same hybris, or spiritual overreaching, Semnani perceives an ending of Abraham's pilgrimage before its proper time: a premature birth, or even a miscarriage, of the spiritual offspring whose seed was placed in the subtle center of the heart, the “Abraham of your being.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01532

Indeed, the “mystery of the hidden mystery” (ghayb al-khafî—Semnani often calls the subtle organs, the latîfa, “mysteries,” ghayb) surrounds and encloses the five mysteries preceding it: spirit, higher consciousness, heart, vital soul, and body.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01533

But this hidden mystery is itself surrounded and enclosed by the Mystery of Mysteries (ghayb al-ghoyûb), the mystery of the true divine center within you (ghayb al-latîfat al-haqqîya). What occurs in Christian dogma, as Semnani understands it, and in Hallaj's cry “I am God” (Anâ'l-Haqq), is a premature interruption of growth and maturation: an initiation that has failed (compare Book I, Chapter VII, §4, above).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01534

That failed initiation is the one that should have led to the birth and recognition of the True Self: the person of your real Self as the organ of the divine within you (anâ'îyat haqqî-ka). The “Jesus of your being” is no more responsible for this failure than Jesus son of Mary is responsible for official Christology.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01535
But the region of your being embodied by that subtle organ is precisely where the danger arises—the same danger confronting both the Sufi and the Christian.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01536

Here Semnani offers an extended explanation. Every latîfa has its corresponding revelation, its unveiling of the self, from the self still bound to bodily life in the first two subtle centers up to the divine Self, the “Glorified One,” the “Muhammad of your being.” The danger arises when the Self “appears” (tajallî) at the level of the hidden mystery, the latîfat al-khafîya.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01537

Conversely, it arises when the secret of this latîfa is unveiled to a self not yet entirely purified of intoxication—of the unconsciousness that clouds and distorts perception at the level of the first two latîfa, the subtle organ of the body and that of the vital soul. A lower mode of perception is still at work, which is why we can speak of a failed initiation.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01538

Christians, in Semnani's account, did not perceive at the level of the hidden mystery (latîfat al-khafîya) the mystery of the divine manifestation: the Holy Spirit appearing visibly to Mary as Gabriel, and breathing into her so that Jesus becomes Rûh Allah, the Spirit of God. They understood it instead on the level of the evidence available to the first two latîfa.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01539

Or, to put it another way: their dogma makes the one God be born materially “on earth,” whereas the “Jesus of your being” is the mystery of your spiritual birth, your heavenly ascent. They spoke of fatherhood, motherhood, and sonship; they asserted a “third of three” (5:77), bringing the relationships of three persons into the mystery of the One who is essentially one. They remained within the kinds of relationship that ordinary consciousness can grasp in the outer world.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01540

They did not penetrate to the sea of the Jabarût, where the points or centers of Knowledge, Will, and Power emerge. (In Semnani's thought these three names designate aspects of a cosmology to which we shall return.) Christians made the first the essence of the Creator, the second his Son, and the third the Holy Spirit. There are, of course, intermediaries (wasâ'it) in the world of Mystery, for divine action always takes place through mediations.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01541

But to conceive those mediations on the model of generation in the sensory world is to see nothing beyond that world. It is, as the old proverb says, to believe that “beyond 'Abadan there is no other town.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01542

Thus one declares Jesus to be the son of God, just as the Jews had come to declare 'Uzayr (Ezra) the son of God (9:30). According to Semnani, the same illusion threatens anyone who, while still spiritually imperfect, reaches the degrees corresponding to the subtle center of the secret (the fourth latîfa, the “Moses of your being”) and the center of the hidden mystery (the fifth latîfa, the “Jesus of your being”).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01543
To save the mystic who, by proclaiming “I am God,” brings divinity down to the level of an earthly human being, Semnani believes the mystic must be “lifted” to a higher spiritual station.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01544

There the nature of the true Self is revealed: a self of which divinity is not an attribute, but which serves as the organ of divine manifestation, because it can become the mirror in which that manifestation occurs and can be filled with it entirely. This is the secret of being “beloved of God”—the state of which God says, concerning the one he loves, “I am the eye with which he sees, the hand with which he touches,” and so forth.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01545

That is the true meaning of the spiritual perspective overturned by the illusion of Anâ'l-Haqq, “I am God”: the illusion of a Moon brought to incandescence by the Sun's light and crying, “I am the sun!” (We have encountered this image before, both in Suhrawardi's Tale of the Crimson Archangel and among the Hurufis.) Here again is the contrast between a way of thinking centered on divine manifestations and a way of thinking centered on incarnation; between an event experienced in vision and one that enters material history and belongs to the past.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01546

This contrast inspires Semnani's extraordinary reading of the Qur'anic verse (4:156) that contains, as we know, the most explicitly “docetist” claim in Qur'anic Christology: “They did not kill him, they did not crucify him ... God raised him to Himself.” This “raising to God” presents the same contrast as Enoch's ascent—when he is invested as the heavenly Anthropos, the archetypal human being, in the divine fullness or Pleroma—set against an Incarnation entering the material reality of earthly history.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01547

The question is plain: does divine humanity come to fulfillment on earth, or rather “in Heaven”? Semnani in effect prescribes a radical cure of “docetism” for the Christian and the misguided Sufi alike, because both, in his judgment, misunderstand what divine manifestations mean: one declares that Jesus is God; the other cries “I am God.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01548

Just as the Gnostic Christology echoed by the Qur'anic verse makes any claim that “God is dead” meaningless and harmless in advance, so the “Jesus of your being” must be raised to the level of the latîfat al-haqqîya, if your initiation is to be completed and you are to be saved from error.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01549

Just as Jesus had to be “raised to God”—lifted, like Enoch, out of the history of the outer, visible world, thereby depriving any worldly power claiming his authority of its foundation—and just as, from the heavenly place to which he was raised, he must return with the Mahdi, the Imam who is the flower of the prophetic lineage, to summon his people to the pure hanîfî religion: so too the “Jesus of your being” must be “raised” by the attraction of divine ecstasy to your latîfat al-haqqîya, until the Friend in the absolute sense makes you a confidant of the mysteries of his essence.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01550

“Until then, do not yield to the illusion that you have arrived and been made perfect through the Manifestation (tajallî) of the subtle reality or mystery of your Self, as it appears to the subtle organ of your hidden mystery.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01551

Abraham's journey must be completed. That is what it means to hear the Qur'anic verses “through the Jesus of your being.” It allows you, when the most holy Light reveals itself, to banish all empty self-glorification from your mind and answer, as Jesus himself answers in the Qur'an: “You know what is within me, but I do not know what is within You. For You are the One who knows the mysteries” (5:116).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01552

“From now on, whenever you hear anything God says to his friend the Prophet, or any allusion concerning him, hear and perceive it through the subtle organ of the divine within you (latîfat al-haqqîya)”—that is, through the “Muhammad of your being.” To understand this designation, we must recall how Semnani imagines the psycho-cosmic formation of the subtle organs, and the sources and influences from which arises the one that realizes the perfect humanity of the Nabî, the prophet, within the spiritual seeker's person. It is in this subtle center that the heavenly human being takes full shape.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01553

Here, too, the subtle body “acquired” through the mystic's spiritual practice reaches its full stature. This “acquired body” (jism moktasab) is essential to Semnani's understanding of the human being; we shall return to it later. It develops like an embryo inside the physical body, which is destined to perish and serves, as it were, as its surrounding membrane.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01554

In turn, this subtle body is like a womb containing the “essential heart” (qalb haqîqî, the Abraham of your being). That heart is the shell cast upon the waves of the human sea, yet it shelters the subtle reality of your true person, capable of serving as the mirror (al-mir'âya) in which the divine becomes manifest.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01555
Two themes of fundamental importance for Semnani's entire spirituality are thus stated.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01556

First, the “spiritual body,” whose formation requires the participation of every organ of the subtle centers, and which surrounds the spiritual child born as the offspring of the “Abraham of your being.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01557

Second, the “mirror,” the speculum: a favored image of this speculative mysticism, because in the mirror the true appearance of divine manifestations is preserved from premature materialization, which betrays a failed initiation. Together, these themes express the concern of a spiritual school whose whole expectation is shaped by the idea of heavenly ascent. Its aim is not to give God a human body of flesh in which God himself would suffer death, but to ensure the birth and growth of the subtle body: the transformation of the human being into a likeness of the divine.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01558

For this school, it is unthinkable that the One should have to annihilate himself in the human condition of flesh so that a human being might be “raised” to the unseen realm of heavenly existence. If the mystic never awakened from the intoxication of “I am God,” that cry would reverse the direction of the ascent and merely foreshadow the tragedy of “God is dead.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01559
By contrast, the mystery of the speculum, the image in the mirror, offers the only way to recognize identity within difference and difference within identity without reducing the one to the other.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01560

And so our shaykh contemplates this subtle body, crowned by the organ of the Self in which the divine appears, as a mystical Sinai: a mountain radiant with purity and the brilliance of divine flashes, a mountain that is the substance of this latîfa. This subtle organ is at once knower and known, contemplator and contemplated, because its nature is that of a Mirror. It is also the “heart” (qalb), the “land of safety” (al-balad al-amîn), protected from demonic incursions and seductions. Here stands the most holy Temple (Bayt Allah al-harâm), of which the Book says: “Whoever enters it is henceforth safe.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01561

Summing up this part of the prologue to his Qur'anic commentary, Semnani insists: “Be certain that each of the seven centers or subtle organs of your being has a people composed of the faculties belonging specifically to that center. All the faculties that are well balanced and established in harmony form the believing people ... All the disordered faculties that persist in their disorder form the unbelieving people.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01562

Through this inner imagery, our shaykh can draw a correspondence between the prophets' roles in the “world of horizons” and their roles in the inner world of the individual person. It also enables him to describe, in moving terms, his experience of the rebellions of “his own unbelieving people” against the message brought to them by the “Muhammad of his being.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01563

“Each subtle center or organ is one of the prophets who appeared upon the horizons after Adam and called humanity to the religion of their father Adam, until the turn of prophecy came to Noah”. So it continues from prophet to prophet, until the coming of Ahmad (Paracletos–Periclytos), the Seal of the Prophets, beloved of the Lord of the Worlds, whose sharî'at, or revealed Law, supersedes the other Laws.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01564

The same is true of the soul's inner world. The spiritual organism grows through the seven latîfa, each corresponding to one of the seven prophets. The mystic recognizes the stages of that growth through visions of colored lights, each belonging to one subtle center—visions that Semnani studied with particular care. All spiritual wayfarers (sâlikân) see these lights at the successive stations of their journey. They are the delicate veils enveloping each latîfa; their characteristic colors reveal to the wayfarer the stage reached in spiritual growth and travel.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01565

The light of the body (the Adam of your being) is smoky gray, shading toward black; that of the vital soul (Noah) is blue; that of the heart (Abraham) is red; that of higher consciousness (Moses) is white; that of the spirit (David) is yellow; that of the hidden mystery (Jesus) is luminous black, or black light (aswad nûrânî); that of the divine center (Muhammad) is a brilliant green (emerald), for green is the color best suited to the secret of the Mystery of Mysteries (sirr ghayb al-ghoyûb). The following table summarizes the correspondences among the organs of the subtle human constitution, the prophets whose names embody them, and the colored lights by which they are recognized.

Elsewhere we have dealt at much greater length with “colored light-visions” in Najm al-Din Kubra and his school, particularly in Najm Daya Razi. The “luminous black” that here symbolizes the subtle center or organ embodied by Jesus is equivalent to the “black light” (Persian nûr-e siyâh) characteristic of certain visions described by Shams al-Din Lahiji, the commentator on Mahmud Shabestari's Rose Garden of Mystery. Unfortunately, we cannot return to this subject in detail here.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
en-book-4-ch-4-s3
3. “The Angel Gabriel of Your Being”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01568

We have now reached the decisive point on which Semnani's whole doctrine of spiritual interpretation depends. On the one hand, we know that in the “world of horizons”—in the historical time of events beneath the moon—the Prophet Muhammad is the “Seal of Prophecy.” On the other, the seeker is instructed to perceive the meaning of the revelations “in the world of the soul” through the “prophets of his being,” and on the “Sinai of his being” through the “Muhammad of his being.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01569

The passage from the “Muhammad of history” to the “Muhammad of the soul” therefore determines the whole spirituality founded on drawing the Qur'anic revelations inward. Those revelations have seven depths of inner meaning, corresponding to the seven subtle organs or centers of mystical human nature. And once again, the process of bringing them inward confronts us with the question we have met before.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01570

We have seen what this meant in the doctrine of the Ishrâqiyûn, the philosophers of illumination, as described by Sa'in al-Din Turka and developed further in the Dabestân. There, too, prophecy was brought entirely into the inner life, though by a path different from Semnani's seven subtle organs. We were reminded that the Active Intelligence, identical with the Holy Spirit and with Gabriel, the Angel of Revelation, is—as the Tenth Intelligence—the “Seal of Prophecy” at the level of the angelic fullness, or Pleroma.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01571

Consequently, according to the theory of knowledge shared by Avicenna and Suhrawardi, every spiritual seeker who unites with this Intelligence acquires through that union the quality of nabî, prophet, and in turn becomes the “Seal of Prophecy.” The event occurs invisibly in the angelic world. It is a purely spiritual event, not a material fact belonging to historical time (zamân âfâqî). It therefore does nothing to invalidate the title “Seal of Prophecy” belonging to the final prophet in the cycle of prophecy in this world.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01572
But a question then arose. The Ishrâqiyûn realize and make actual the inner meaning of prophecy and the prophetic mission.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01573

Yet it was originally Shiism that defined that inner meaning and determined its content, by declaring the Imam's walâyat—his spiritual guardianship and authority—to be the inner meaning of prophecy. What, then, becomes of walâyat, and of a walâyat without an Imam, when the Ishrâqiyûn reach the reality itself without speaking the name of walâyat or of the Imam? Sa'in al-Din offered a restrained answer: all seekers whose spiritual degree falls short of Shiism live in and represent the imminence of the Hour, but the Hour has not yet dawned.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01574

Semnani's inward approach likewise brings the whole understanding of prophecy into the soul. It would be impossible to realize prophecy's inner meaning more radically than by tracing its different aspects back to the “prophets of your being.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01575

Yet because of his personal formation, Semnani's horizon is not dominated by the questions about knowledge that opened the way for the Ishrâqiyûn. The Active Intelligence, under its various names and in its prophetic function, does not occupy the center of his inner journey as it does for the mystical wayfarer in Suhrawardi's visionary narratives.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01576

Nevertheless, beyond the seven latîfa, or subtle organs, whose prophetic figures together encompass the whole cycle of prophecy by corresponding to each of the seven great prophets sent to reveal a Book, a sharî'at—beyond these seven latîfa, Semnani mentions another, mysterious latîfa that he never explains systematically. He calls it the latîfa jabrâ'eliya. It is a subtle center or organ that, at the summit of prophetic anthropology and by analogy with the other seven latîfa, must be understood as the “Angel Gabriel of your being.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01577

Yet Gabriel, who is the Holy Spirit, is precisely the figure identified by the Ishrâqiyûn and the spiritual knowers ('orafâ) with the philosophers' Active Intelligence, and vice versa. He is the Angel of Knowledge and the Angel of Revelation. This identification illuminates a familiar hadîth: “The learned [or the sages] of Muhammad's community play a role among it analogous to that of the prophets among the people of Israel”. We thus encounter a situation parallel to the one Sa'in al-Din enabled us to examine among the Ishrâqiyûn. Gabriel, the Angel of Knowledge and Revelation, made each of them a nabî.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01578

Yet in the traditional understanding of prophecy, the Angel's role is to reveal the outward meaning to the prophet. The prophetic teaching of the Ishrâqiyûn, by contrast, leads every spiritual seeker into the inward meaning of prophecy. Is the Angel of Revelation, then, the same as the angel of ta'wîl, of inward interpretation? Or should we say that an angelic understanding of knowledge necessarily calls for a corresponding understanding of the Imam's role in knowledge, because the outward (zâhir) calls for the inward (bâtin), and prophecy (nobowwat) calls for spiritual guardianship (walâyat)?
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01579

Now Semnani carries the inward interpretation of prophecy through to its conclusion by making Gabriel himself a latîfa, a subtle organ of mystical human nature. The “Gabriel of your being” is the angel of ta'wîl. And so the earlier question returns: does this also give us the inner meaning of prophecy—that is, the Imam's walâyat—without the Imam? The answer promises to be extraordinarily important for the history of spirituality.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01580

Let us note briefly that this latîfa jabrâ'eliya is also what Semnani calls, with a telling expression, the ostâd ghaybî: the invisible master, the personal master within. When we sense in Semnani an understanding of the Imam that does not speak its own name, the reason may simply be that he has brought the role of the Imam, like that of prophecy, radically into the inner life.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01581

But this inward experience is common to all the spiritual knowers ('orafâ). We already know that in certain meditations on the saying “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord,” the figure of the Imam comes to overlap with that of the self (“whoever knows his Imam”). The lived devotion to the Twelfth Imam, “hidden from the senses but present in the hearts of his faithful,” is eo ipso, by that very fact, a relationship with the ostâd ghaybî.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01582

There is no shortage of testimony to this. Why, then, by leaving unspoken the understanding of the Imam presupposed by his own esoteric teaching, does Semnani seem only to deepen the ambiguity between Shiism and Sufism—an ambiguity that Haydar Amoli would denounce so forcefully a generation later?
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01583

The elements of an answer—or rather, the lines along which we must investigate—are to be sought, first, in Semnani's own religious convictions. What are we to make of the Sunnism he professed? And, at the same time, what are we to make of the devotion he professed toward the Imam? Second, we must look to what constitutes the very essence of the ostâd ghaybî, and to the way this invisible master intervenes within a strictly inward, esoteric perspective—that is, within Semnani's understanding of prophecy as an inner reality.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01584

In short, how is the “Angel Gabriel of your being,” as inward master and invisible guide, also the “Imam of your being,” even though Semnani does not use that term? For “Imam of your being” is precisely the expression that corresponds to bringing the Imam's role inward in Ismaili mysticism and in Twelver Shiism. The comparison would be illuminating.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01585

Although many people in Iran today regard Semnâni as having been a Shiite, the matter is not so simple. Certainly, it would be difficult to exclude him altogether from Shiism, if only because he shared Haydar Âmolî’s conviction that “the Sufis are the true Shiites.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01586

But there is more to it than that. The testimony of Qâzî Nûrollâh Shoshtarî may not be conclusive. Some scholars believe that this devout historian, later honored as Shiism’s “Third Martyr,” sometimes allowed his Shiite fervor to carry him away, claiming certain great figures of the past for the cause of the Imams.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01587

Yet Qâzî Nûrollâh seems in fact to have recognized a “Shiism that dares not speak its name,” and to have judged Semnâni’s case with sensitivity and insight. Among other things, he refers to a treatise by Semnâni of which, unfortunately, we have not yet found a manuscript. On one point of doctrine, however, its teaching agrees perfectly with a passage in the prologue to Semnâni’s Tafsîr: the passage in which he acknowledges that Imam Ali alone possessed the fullness of the Imamate (khilâfat, wirâthat, walâyat).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01588

We shall return to this. It is also striking that when Semnâni quotes a saying of the Fourth Imam, Zayn al-Âbidîn, he follows the Imam’s name with a solemn blessing (taslîm) of the kind customarily used only by Shiites. His position concerning the Twelfth Imam is not that of a Twelver Shiite, but he does accept that the Mahdi must be a descendant of Fâtima and that, after the First Imam, he alone will unite in himself the fullness of the Imamate.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01589

Indeed, as we shall recall later, Semnâni draws from this belief a spirituality entirely consistent with his method of turning religious realities inward: the mystic must bring the spiritual power of the awaited Imam to life within himself. He must not simply wait for the Imam’s coming, but must bring it closer, make it happen. Many spiritual teachers have expressed this same feeling. No less significant is another detail. Throughout a short treatise devoted to the First Imam, published some years ago, Semnâni refers to Imam Ali as “our Imam”—a phrase that comes naturally only to a Shiite.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01590

Finally, as a master of Sufism, Semnâni understands perfectly well what the cycle of walâyat means. If the Qur’an contains every perfection, he tells us, it is because God has established within it both an “outer center” (al-noqtat al-zâhira) and an “inner center” (al-noqtat al-bâtina). Around the latter revolves the cycle of walâyat, once the cycle of prophecy has come to an end. This is why Semnâni repeatedly recalls the solemn words addressed by the Prophet to Ali ibn Abî-Tâlib.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01591

Here—and this is the full significance the tradition acquires among Twelver Shiites and Ismailis alike—the name Ali (the “Exalted,” Excelsus) refers not merely to the historical individual who was Imam, but to the very reality of the Imamate: the eternal Imam. (In the Ismaili writings of the Alamût tradition, this eternal figure is called Melchizedek during the first two periods of the cycle.) The person of the visible Imam is the earthly pole of that reality, its manifestation in this world.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01592

“God Most High said to me: O Mohammad! I sent Ali secretly [invisibly] with the other prophets; with you I have sent him openly [visibly].” The Prophet himself explained these words when he said to Ali: “You stand in relation to me as Aaron stood in relation to Moses.” He also said: “There will be no prophet after me”—so that it might be understood that the door of prophecy is, and remains, closed, whereas the door of walâyat is, and remains, open.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01593

These traditions (hadîth) have an immense and quite definite significance in Shiism. They confirm other traditions proclaiming that a single Light gave rise to both the prophetic mission and the Imamate. These are the outward and inward aspects of the “eternal Muhammadan Reality” (Haqîqat mohammadîya): outwardly, the Prophet’s nobowwat, his prophetic mission; inwardly, the Imam’s walâyat, his spiritual authority and power of initiation. They are, respectively, the proclamation of Revelation and the unveiling of its hidden meaning.
